data: This course examines the psychological, biological, biomedical, and sociotechnical dimensions of self-tracking practices in contemporary digital life. With a central focus on the biological and cognitive mechanisms underlying self-regulation, feedback, and sense-making, the course explores how digital technologies enable a prospective approach to health management, and how they mediate and reshape attention, decision-making, memory, emotion, and embodied experience; the course also  Drawing on perspectives from biology, cognitive neuroscience, behavioral psychology, and cultural theory, students will critically engage with topics such as neurofeedback, affective computing, persuasive design, and the cognitive labor of managing personal data. The course also addresses broader social and ethical implications, including surveillance, inequality, and the politics of measurement. Through interdisciplinary readings and experiential assignments, students will investigate how cognitive processes are both reflected in and transformed by the quantified self.
